planting.note: Pot in a fine bark-and-perlite terrestrial mix in bright shade with warm-to-intermediate temperatures year-round, since this lowland-to-mid-elevation species has no cold-rest requirement.

directions: Native to the Himalayan foothills from northeast India through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam, this species carries plain, deep-green, strap-shaped leaves topped in winter by a single flower with a glossy, varnished texture rare among slipper orchids, its twisted dorsal sepal and coppery-brown petals catching the light like lacquered wood. It is one of the two parent species, alongside Paphiopedilum barbatum, behind Paphiopedilum Harrisianum, raised by Veitch nursery in 1869 and recognized as the first Paphiopedilum hybrid ever bloomed. Keep the fine bark mix evenly moist year-round, since this species has no water-storing pseudobulbs, and provide bright shade with steady warmth rather than a seasonal temperature drop. Established clumps can be divided after flowering to produce new plants.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Pot in a fine bark-and-perlite terrestrial mix in bright shade with warm, humid conditions year-round, matching the lowland Malay Peninsula habitat of this species.

directions: Native to the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and Thailand, this species forms a fan of leaves tessellated in two shades of green and sends up a single flower with a pale, green-and-purple-veined dorsal sepal above petals edged in bristly, dark warts, the beard-like fringe that gives the species its name. Along with Paphiopedilum villosum, it was one of the two parent species crossed by Veitch nursery in 1869 to raise Paphiopedilum Harrisianum, generally regarded as the first Paphiopedilum hybrid ever bloomed. Keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, since this species has no pseudobulbs to buffer dry spells, and provide warm, humid, shaded conditions rather than the cooler regime some other slipper orchids need. Feed lightly at quarter strength with regular waterings since the plant stays continuously rooted.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Repot back-bulb divisions into a coarse bark-based cymbidium mix in a shallow pot; Cymbidium eburneum benefits from a cool autumn night drop to help initiate winter-to-spring flower spikes.

directions: Native to the Himalayan foothills of northeast India, Nepal, and Myanmar east to Hainan, this epiphytic species carries short pseudobulbs and narrow, grassy leaves, sending up a short spike bearing one or two large, waxy, intensely fragrant white flowers with a yellow-stained lip in late winter to spring. It stands behind Cymbidium Alexanderi as a grandparent through the intermediate hybrid Cymbidium eburneo-lowianum, which Sir George Holford crossed with Cymbidium insigne in 1911; the resulting grex's spontaneous tetraploid 'Westonbirt' clone became a foundational breeding parent for the large-flowered cymbidium hybrids grown commercially today. Grow in bright, filtered light with a distinct cool snap in autumn to set spikes, watering freely while pseudobulbs are actively growing and allowing the mix to dry more once flowers appear. Repot only every two to three years, since cymbidiums bloom best when slightly pot-bound.

planting.note: Grow in fine bark or sphagnum in a small pot; this species tolerates more direct sun and less humidity than typical Phalaenopsis, reflecting its naturally sunnier, more exposed habitat.

directions: Native to Thailand, Malaysia, and Indochina, this compact species carries thick, fleshy, often purple-tinged leaves and an upright, branching spike of small, slightly fragrant magenta to lavender-pink flowers that reopen in flushes over many months rather than one seasonal bloom. It was crossed with Phalaenopsis violacea in 1963 by Clarelen Orchids to produce the classic grex Doritaenopsis Kenneth Schubert, a foundation parent behind much of the modern purple and blue Phalaenopsis breeding line, and its stronger sun and heat tolerance carries through into that hybrid and its descendants. Grow warm and humid in a well-drained bark or sphagnum mix, watering as the medium approaches dryness and providing brighter light than most Phalaenopsis tolerate. Modern taxonomy folds Doritis into Phalaenopsis, so it is also listed in some references as Phalaenopsis pulcherrima.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

common_name: Angel Bells Cattleya (Historic White Cattleya Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow in bright, filtered light in a coarse bark mix typical of standard Cattleya culture, allowing the mix to approach dryness between thorough waterings.

directions: Cattleya Angel Bells is a white-flowered Cattleya hybrid best known today as one of the two parent grexes, crossed with Cattleya Claesiana by Ben Kodama of Hawaii in 1982, behind the fragrant hybrid Cattleya Hawaiian Wedding Song, a long-standing favorite among cut-flower and wedding-bouquet growers for its pure white, long-lasting blooms. Grow it like a standard Cattleya, in bright, filtered light with good air movement and a coarse, fast-draining bark mix, letting the medium approach dryness between thorough waterings. Allow a brief, slightly cooler and drier rest after each new growth matures to help set the next flowering cycle. As with other white-flowered Cattleya breeding lines, strong light is needed for compact growth and reliable bloom, since plants grown in heavy shade tend toward lush foliage with few flowers.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

common_name: Claesiana Cattleya (Historic White Cattleya Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow in bright, filtered light in a coarse bark mix typical of standard Cattleya culture, allowing the mix to approach dryness between thorough waterings.

directions: Cattleya Claesiana is the second parent grex, alongside Cattleya Angel Bells, behind the fragrant 1982 Ben Kodama hybrid Cattleya Hawaiian Wedding Song, a snow-white cut-flower favorite noted for blooms that last six to eight weeks and typically flower twice yearly. Grow it under standard Cattleya conditions, with bright, filtered light, good air movement, and a coarse, fast-draining bark mix, watering thoroughly and letting the medium dry somewhat between waterings. Provide a brief cooler, drier rest once each new growth matures to encourage reliable flowering the following cycle. Like other historically important white-flowered Cattleya parent lines, it rewards strong light with more compact growth and heavier bloom than plants grown in shade.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Grow warm with bright indirect light in a small pot of coarse bark mix, watering freely during active summer growth on fleshy, cane-type pseudobulbs.

directions: Dendrobium Enobi Komachi is a hard-cane Dendrobium hybrid grown for fleshy, upright cane-type pseudobulbs, and it was crossed with Dendrobium Laguna Princess by Japanese breeder K. Karasawa in 1996 to produce the widely grown grex Dendrobium Enobi Purple, carrying a dozen or more bright magenta-purple flowers in succession along its spikes. Grow warm with bright indirect light, watering regularly and feeding during active summer growth as new canes elongate. Allow canes to dry somewhat more between waterings during cooler months, since continued warmth and moisture at that stage tends to promote keiki growth along the canes rather than flower buds. Resume regular watering and feeding once new growths and roots emerge in spring.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Grow warm with bright indirect light in a small pot of coarse bark mix, watering freely during active summer growth on fleshy, cane-type pseudobulbs.

directions: Dendrobium Laguna Princess is the second parent, alongside Dendrobium Enobi Komachi, behind the 1996 Japanese-bred hard-cane hybrid Dendrobium Enobi Purple, whose dense, evenly spaced magenta-purple flowers and fleshy cane-type pseudobulbs trace back to both parent grexes. Grow warm with bright indirect light, watering and fertilizing freely while new canes are actively elongating through summer. Reduce watering somewhat as canes mature and into cooler months, since premature or continuous watering at that stage tends to trigger keiki growth along the cane rather than the following season's flower buds. Resume regular watering once new roots and growths appear in spring.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

common_name: Madame Rattana Vanda (Historic Strap-Leaf Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow in a slatted basket or mounted with roots exposed to air, in strong light and high humidity typical of Vanda-alliance culture.

directions: Vanda Madame Rattana is a strap-leaf Vanda hybrid best known as one of the two parents, crossed with Vanda Kasem's Delight by R.F. Orchids in Florida in 1984, behind Vanda Robert's Delight, a hybrid that has since produced numerous AOS-awarded color forms in the large, flat, rounded flower shape typical of strap-leaf Vanda breeding. Grow in strong light with high humidity and daily watering or misting in warm weather, letting the exposed roots dry briefly between soakings. Best grown in a slatted basket or mounted to allow full root aeration, matching the culture of the modern hybrids it helped produce. Like other strap-leaf Vanda parent lines, it rewards consistent warmth and strong light with more compact growth and more reliable flowering.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

common_name: Elisabethae Phalaenopsis (Historic White Moth Orchid Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in coarse bark, allowing the mix to dry slightly between waterings, in a modest fan of thick, glossy leaves.

directions: Phalaenopsis Elisabethae is a complex descendant of Phalaenopsis amabilis that was crossed with Phalaenopsis Katherine Siegwart by Duke Farms of Somerville, New Jersey and registered in November 1940 as Phalaenopsis Doris, one of the most influential white-flowered Phalaenopsis lines of the twentieth century. Through Doris, its broad, flat, white-flowered form helped establish the benchmark shape that later breeders used repeatedly in developing the large, round-flowered white Phalaenopsis hybrids common in the trade today. Grow in bright indirect light with warm temperatures and coarse bark, allowing the mix to dry slightly between thorough waterings. Keep humidity moderate to high, since, like its modern descendants, it forms a modest fan of thick, glossy leaves without pseudobulbs to store water reserves.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

common_name: Katherine Siegwart Phalaenopsis (Historic White Moth Orchid Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in coarse bark, allowing the mix to dry slightly between waterings, in a modest fan of thick, glossy leaves.

directions: Phalaenopsis Katherine Siegwart is, like Phalaenopsis Elisabethae, a complex descendant of Phalaenopsis amabilis, and the two were crossed by Duke Farms and registered in November 1940 as Phalaenopsis Doris, a grex that went on to produce a string of individually awarded clones and became a benchmark white-flowered line through the twentieth century. Its contribution to Doris's broad, flat, pure white flowers with a touch of yellow and red in the lip helped set the form that later breeders used repeatedly in developing today's large, round-flowered white Phalaenopsis hybrids. Grow in bright indirect light with steady warmth and coarse bark, letting the mix dry slightly between waterings. Maintain moderate to high humidity, since this parent line, like its modern descendants, forms a compact fan of thick leaves with no pseudobulbs for water storage.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register
